speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: RED CROSS REQUEST FOR AID FOR NIGERIA
speechtext: Has the Government of Canada received a request from the International Red Cross to provide relief for the victims of the civil war in Nigeria and, if so (a) what was the nature of any such request (b) when was such request made (c) what was the response?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RED CROSS REQUEST FOR AID FOR NIGERIA
speechtext:
1. Yes.
1 (a), (b) and (c). On May 28, 1968 an appeal was made by the International Committee of the Red Cross to the government of Canada through the Canadian Red Cross Society. The immediate response was a cash grant of $60,000 provided to the ICRC for relief work in areas of Nigeria where the need was greatest.
At a meeting July 12 with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, representatives of Canadian voluntary organizations, including the Canadian Red Cross, invited a Canadian government contribution to Nigerian relief and drew attention to the ICRC's need for transport aircraft. The Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that the Canadian government would be prepared to consider a request from the Canadian Red Cross Society for an aircraft if the agreement of the parties concerned (the Nigerian government, the ICRC and the rebel authorities) could be obtained, and satisfactory arrangements made for its use. The Canadian government also, shortly thereafter, allocated $500,000 in food aid for distribution by the ICRC in the areas of greatest need in Nigeria.
In August, the ICRC developed a program involving agreed daylight flights into rebel held (Biafran) territory. The government learned that the ICRC would, through the Canadian Red Cross Society, ask for Canadian Hercules aircraft to participate. As agreement was not reached with both sides in the conflict, the daylight airlift was not possible and the Canadian government was not able to accede to this request.
On September 17, another allocation of $500,000 was made for food to be distributed in the needy areas in Nigeria. On September 26, following a meeting between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the national commissioner of the Canadian Red Cross Society, an offer of a Canadian armed forces Hercules aircraft was made to the ICRC for use in territory under the control of the Nigerian government. The aircraft in

November 20, 1968
Questions
question arrived in Lagos on October 14 and was put at the disposal of the ICEC.
Following discussions between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Commissioner for External Affairs of Nigeria, on October 8, in New York, agreement was reached by which the Nigerian government would allow Canadian armed forces aircraft to operate in Nigeria, including rebel held territory, for the purpose of transporting relief supplies on behalf of the ICRC. A Canadian armed forces Hercules scheduled for use between the island of Fernando Po (Equatorial Guinea) and rebel held territory received clearances from Equatorial Guinea on October 26 and was put at the disposal of the ICRC on arrival there on October 26.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: SKI FACILITIES, CAPE BRETON HIGHLANDS PARK
speechtext:
1. Since 1958, there has been constant pressure from the Sydney Board of Trade, the Cape Breton Ski Club, numerous private individuals, and members of parliament, to have this department undertake ski development in Cape Breton Highlands national park. Investigations by departmental officials in 1961 and in 1966 indicated that the best potential location within the park for a ski development was South Mountain. Their surveys merely confirmed the technical suitability of the area for skiing and were not comprehensive studies of development feasibility. The decision to invite development proposals was made in June 1968, and was based on the report of a private consulting firm which examined the feasibility of a ski area in the park last year. The location selected for the establishment of these facilities, recommended by departmental officials and the consulting firm, was the northern face of South Mountain.
2.	(a) Originally it was planned to provide only basic facilities such as an access road, parking area, a rope tow and a warming hut. However as a result of the consultants' report on the development potential of the area, the demand for skiing facilities, and economic feasibility, it was apparent that a more comprehensive development could be considered, (b) In general, the changes concern the extent of development. The present call for tenders provides for more extensive development of the site in two stages. The first phase of development will include a day lodge with cafeteria facilities and a ski shop, a 2,200 foot T-Bar lift, a 5-run trail and slope system, and parking for 125 cars. Additional ski runs and facilities will be provided at a later date as the demand and profit warrant.
3.	The earlier work on planning ski facilities at Cape Breton Highlands national park was concerned with selecting a possible site with very modest facilities. This plan was not developed to the point of costing. With the

present program, the estimated financial involvement of the federal government is $13,000 for an access road and parking facilities. The balance of the costs of development will be borne by the successful tenderer for the ski facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to make a very long opening statement since there was a thorough discussion of a number of matters affecting the department when the amendment to the Judges Act was before the house. I anticipate that when the criminal law omnibus bill returns to the house there will be ample scope to review the criminal law.
Since the main estimates of the Department of Justice for 1967-68 were considered in some detail by the standing committee on justice and legal affairs, with the consequence that no extensive statement was made before the house, I think it would be in order for me to make a short general statement concerning this year's estimates of the department.
Hon. members will know that the Government Organization Act of 1966, which was proclaimed on October 1 of that year, transferred to other ministers various branches of the public service that previously fell under the superintendence of the Department of Justice. The result of these changes was that the Department of Justice now has the same responsibilities that it had under the original statute following confederation in 1868, and those duties now remain virtually unaltered.
As matters presently stand, Mr. Chairman, responsibility for the institution and conduct of prosecutions within the federal field of jurisdiction remains with the Attorney General of Canada. This is true even though the supervision of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police now rests with my colleague, the Solicitor General.
Notwithstanding this, Mr. Chairman, prosecutions resulting from police investigations within the federal jurisdiction continue to be the responsibility of the Attorney General of Canada, and are conducted by him through his officials and agents. This situation applies as well to prosecutions under the Combines Investigation Act. While ministerial functions relating to that act are now transferred to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission reports directly to parliament

November 20, 1968
Supply-Justice
through that minister, the decision to prosecute and the conduct of a prosecution in any particular combine, merger, monopoly, restraint of trade or price fixing case continues to be the responsibility of the Attorney General.
So, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada continues to be responsible for providing legal services to the government generally, as set out in the Department of Justice Act. In fact, the Attorney General is lawyer for every department of the government service. His functions are advisory. He is charged with conducting litigation on behalf of the people of Canada. He is charged with advising on the drafting of legislation for every government department, and so on.
This year's estimates show an increase in staff amounting to 72 additional positions and a proportionate increase in the amount provided for salaries. I would not want the committee to think that this increased number of 72 positions represents an equivalent increase in the over-all establishment of the government. It has been made clear that it is the intention of the government to provide an integrated legal service along the lines generally recommended in the Glassco report. That is to say, the Department of Justice will now be responsible in a general way for the legal functions that are carried on in every department of government, and to that end we are in the process of integrating the legal services of the government.
This policy, Mr. Chairman, is reflected in the fact that 27 of these new positions represent transfers from other departments-one from Industry, one from Finance, 14 from Defence Production and 11 from National Revenue, customs and excise. This in turn results in an equivalent reduction in the estimates of the other departments involved.
The balance of these positions, apart from some nine in the minister's office, which were not included in previous estimates as a result of former Treasury Board policy but now are included, result from support of the positions that have been transferred

nine secretarial positions have been established for this purpose-and increase in the strength of the department not only in Ottawa but in the regional offices that we plan to set up in major regions of the country.

Honourable members know full well that we have established in Montreal an almost

independent office to deal with the department's business in the metropolis of Quebec and Canada. There is also another regional office in Toronto and one in Vancouver. We intend to set up other regional offices, perhaps one in Winnipeg and the other in Halifax. This is the indication of some decentralization in the management of the department's business with a view to ensuring quicker action and a more accessible justice for the citizens of these areas.

Each of these offices has a professional staff of roughly a dozen lawyers, and these offices have been found to work out very well in practice. It is the intention of the government, as I say, to continue to extend the regional office idea so as to facilitate the work of the department. These local offices can handle claims and prosecutions and provide on the spot legal advice for the various federal government departments that have offices in such cities or districts.
Apart from the work of the department as I have described it, Mr. Chairman, the Department of Justice concerns itself with the subject of law reform. In the very near future I will be reintroducing a bill that will make extensive revisions in the Criminal Code, and I will also be introducing a completely revised and new Expropriation Act. We intend to set up a new research branch in the Department of Justice that will be charged with the reform of the law and the revision of statutes.
I mentioned when I spoke to the students at Osgoode Hall that we were going to set up within the next two years a national law reform commission charged with reviewing the entire area of federal statutes and the criminal law. I hope too that we will have a permanent statute revision next year. The purpose of the research branch of the department will be to co-ordinate and to liaise with the national law reform commission, with institutes of criminology across the country, with law faculties and, of course, the profession in general.

I agree with the hon. member that it is most awkward for the citizen, and especially in the case of an expert, to look up something in the statutes. He has to read them all year by year, since 1952. There is under consideration in the department a complete revision of the Canada Shipping Act and the Admiralty Act. In conjunction with the Department of Transport we
Supply-Justice
hope to bring in a new maritime code. This is a long term project to be developed continuously in the next five or ten years. After that we will have a rationalized code in Canada for maritime matters.
On other occasions I hope to bring forward revisions to the Exchequer Court Act which will probably provide for some means of relieving some of the pressure that is put on the Supreme Court of Canada. Proceedings must now be by way of a petition for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The revisions will be in the form of an appellate division of this court and a reform in the administrative law. We shall consider the process of judicial review of administrative tribunals.
These are examples of what we believe to be relatively major undertakings to be undertaken by the Department of Justice in the area of law reform. It is the view of this government that even greater efforts in this area ought to be made, and I therefore intend to bring forward legislation in the months to come that will be directed to this end. I look forward with interest to what hon. members of the committee have to say and I shall do my best to answer their questions.

Mr. Chairman, we thank the minister for his introductory statement. He has attempted to explain why his departmental estimates are considerably higher than they were last year. I suggest that there are still unanswered questions, and the committee would like to hear answers to those questions.
The minister explained that it would be the policy of the department to establish 72 additional positions within the department. I notice that the estimates this year provide for a vote of $185,000 for professional and special services, while the amount for that item last year was only $50,000. In 1966-67 the amount applicable here was only $10,000. If the minister is to establish 72 additional positions in the department, why does he need the vote of $185,000 to provide for professional and special services? Surely some of those 72 additional men who are to be put on the department's payroll could take care of a good many of the professional services the department is to be expected to supply.
I notice in vote 1 an item of $1,088,000 for the publication of departmental reports and other material. In 1967-68, that is last year, that vote amounted to only $40,000. I think the committee is entitled to know why the amount has jumped from $40,000 to $1,088,000. Another item had to do with travelling

November 20, 1968

expenses. I presume that has reference to travelling expenses for the officials of the department, since judges' travelling expenses are provided for under another item. This year travelling expenses are up by $19,000. Accommodation provided by the Department of Public Works is increased by a figure of $447,000.
The fact is that the estimates of the Department of Justice this year are $4,778,500 higher than they were last year. I suggest that in these days of so-called austerity, of cutbacks by governments, when provinces are told they are practically on their own from now on, it is strange to find that in the Department of Justice, which is a comparatively small department of government, spending estimates for this year are $5 million above those of last year. Before the estimates pass I think the minister must give us a detailed explanation of how this increase has come about.
We hear the minister say that he intends to proceed with proposed amendments to the Criminal Code. This is a very, very important piece of legislation and one which at some time or other could touch virtually every citizen of this country. The amendments were introduced last year under bill C-195. That was an omnibus bill which purported to be an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and to make certain consequential amendments to the Combines Investigation Act and the Customs Tariff. That is legislation of a very wide scope. The Prime Minister said that the law has no place in the bedrooms of the nation; but these proposals are so wide in scope that if they do not make their appearance in the bedrooms of the nation they will affect almost every other phase of our living.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We have not as yet seen this new bill. If it contains everything that was contained in the previous bill C-195, which was submitted last year, it will contain much that is good. The bill contains at the moment some things with which all of us might not be able to agree. We therefore hoped we would not be placed in a position where we would have to vote against the entire bill, including those parts which we considered to be good, simply because there were other parts with which we could not agree. The former minister of justice, the present Prime Minister, indicated last session that the house would be required to vote upon this omnibus bill in its entirety-that it would not be broken up. Since

then there has of course, been a change in the administration. The present minister gave us some hope when he intimated that he would like to see the bill divided so that it could be voted on in sections. He expressed himself to that extent. But apparently the great white father who sits in the seat of the prime minister decreed otherwise, and the poor Minister of Justice was faced with the choice of either falling into line or picking up his marbles and going home.
I do not think that even Adolf Hitler ruled with a firmer hand than does the present Prime Minister, nor do I believe there has ever been a more docile group of ministers than those who hold office now. If the medical profession ever gets around to doing spine transplants there will be an open field over there, because these men are spineless. Why cannot the Minister of Justice be an exception to this general rule? I am sure he is convinced in his own mind that this bill should be broken down and voted upon in separate parts. He knows very well that this is the proper way in which to proceed. He knows very well that this is the manner in which the majority of members would like to see it dealt with. I suggest he be not afraid any more of the great white father. The Prime Minister is not going to fire him; he is too good a minister. The Prime Minister will not let him go. I am afraid that the whole spectrum of American politics looms high over this executive decision by Mr. Rusk. Even our former secretary of state for external affairs, Hon. Paul Martin, challenged Mr. Rusk's position when, on March 27 of this year, he was reported to have said that the ground on which Mr. Rusk refused to return Banks to Canada-
-does not exist under the terms of the extradition convention between Canada and the United States.
In other words he argued that Mr. Rusk probably did not have the authority-certainly did not have the judicial authority-to over-rule the decision of the commissioner.
This man Hal Banks is a fugitive from justice. He must be returned to this country, if there is any way of getting him back here, to stand trial. He skipped his bail. He is free today because in the first place he was rich enough to put up $25,000 bail. The sum of $25,000 did not mean anything to Hal Banks. Then he left Canada and, in essence, defied the courts to bring him back. I hope in all sincerity that Hal Banks has not got a friend in court so far as the government is concerned. I hope the minister will do his very best and co-operate with the senator from New Mexico to have this man returned to Canada.

If there is any possible chance, and I think there is, that the executive decision of Dean Rusk can now be over-ruled by the new executive, then I suggest nothing should be done to hinder that being accomplished. This is a very important matter. I repeat that this man is a fugitive from justice and the government-no government-should do anything at all to help him. Had he been a poor man he would probably still be languishing in jail. He is free now only because he was able to put up $25,000.
That, Mr. Chairman, leads me to the next matter on which I would like to comment briefly. As a practising lawyer and as a former attorney general, this is a matter which has always given me quite a bit of concern. I refer to the matter of detention after arrest, and of course the question of bail. I feel that this is presently receiving the attention of the department.
My experience in the field of criminal law, both as a prosecuting attorney and as a defence counsel, has led me to believe that in many cases the police unnecessarily arrest a person, take him into custody and lodge him in jail when the circumstances of the case do not warrant such drastic action. This has resulted in a great deal of unnecessary hardship and very considerable personal inconvenience and embarrassment, when a summons in the first instance would have been all that was necessary to make sure that a man appeared for his trial.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Chairman, that arrests are not in some cases necessary. An arrest is quite often necessary not only for the protection of society but also for the protection of the person arrested. But there are occasions when persons who are very well known, who are large property owners, and where there would be absolutely no question about turning up the next day for trial, have been placed under arrest. Such a person, I maintain, should not be arrested in the first instance but should merely be summoned. I am afraid that very often an arrest is made, with the result that the person concerned is punished by the very arrest itself. This is punishment in itself, even before he is tried and convicted. He is punished once he is placed in custody, and this of course is contrary to the whole spirit of our laws.
I am of the opinion that possibly the Criminal Code leaves a police officer with very little discretion. If a policeman decides to detain a person he is almost obliged to arrest him and place him in jail. I suggest that this matter should be studied by the law officers
November 20, 1968



of the crown with a view to suggesting certain amendments to the Criminal Code, if necessary, which would allow policemen to use discretion in certain cases. I am not suggesting that all persons should be immediately released. I am suggesting, however, that the arresting officer should be empowered to exercise some discretion in matters of this kind. Very often, as I say, the arrest causes not only inconvenience and humiliation but also is done at some considerable cost to the public. Every time a man is arrested there naturally is some expense involved.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I have looked into this in a rather cursory manner and it would seem to me that if we could amend section 435 of the code to make the officer's right to arrest without a warrant dependant not only upon his having reasonable and probable grounds for believing that an offence has been committed, but also upon its being reasonable for him to arrest rather than to summon, this would leave him some discretion if he should feel in his own mind that the reasonable thing to do is to release the man immediately and issue a summons. I believe if we were to amend section 435 of the code we could probably accomplish this purpose.
A number of other changes could be introduced into the code. Unless these changes are made we will find that the summons procedure will not be used extensively and that the police will continue to arrest almost indiscriminately. This is actually what happens. A study of a sampling of 6,000 cases was made a few years ago and it was revealed at that time that 90 per cent of those charged with Criminal Code offences were arrested, while less than 10 per cent were summonsed. It was also revealed in this study-and this is an alarming situation-that approximately 85 per cent of those arrested were kept in police custody until their first court appearance. In many instances this involved a substantial period of time.
In one division in the city of Toronto, for example, over 80 per cent of those who were booked between seven o'clock in the morning and midnight were kept in police custody for more than 10 hours before their court appearance, and then they were required to raise bail. This would seem to me, in many cases, to be an injustice, because of the 80 per cent of these men or women who were booked I think I would be safe in assuming a very large percentage were responsible citizens
Supply-Justice
who could have been released immediately and would have appeared in court the next day on a summons. In these cases it would not have been necessary for them to have been kept in custody for a period of up to 10 hours and be faced with the inconvenience of attempting to find someone who would put up their bail.
This leads me to my next point, the question of bail. Here I suggest that a change in the law is very definitely needed and long overdue. The provisions for the ordering of bail prior to trial, in all offences whether indictable or summary conviction, are found in section 451 of the Criminal Code. They are identical to the provisions relating to preliminary inquiries. Section 451 of the Criminal Code provides:
A justice acting under this Part may (a) order that an accused, at any time before he has been' committed for trial, be admitted to bail
(i)	upon the accused entering into a recognizance in form 28 before him or any other justice, with sufficient sureties in such amount as he or that justice directs,
(ii)	upon the accused entering into a recognizance in form 28 before him or any other justice and depositing an amount that he or that justice directs, or
(iii)	upon the accused entering into his own recognizance in form 28 before him or any other justice in such amount as he or that justice directs without any deposit;
It is clear, therefore, that the ordering of bail is a judicial act. It must be done by a judge, a magistrate or a justice. The amount of bail and whether or not it is to be granted at all is decided by the justice. I am not levelling any criticism at the men who make the decisions, but I believe it is pretty generally recognized, particularly in the smaller jurisdictions, that some of the justices who make these decisions are not trained in the law. I know this does not apply in the major centres. We would probably not find this situation in Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver or Calgary. However, in some of the smaller areas there are justices who, although they do their best, are not trained in the law and for that reason perhaps cannot properly appreciate the situations with which they are faced, and therefore perhaps are not in a position to exercise properly the discretion vested in them. I agree that the law requires that before exercising this discretion the justice should obtain as much information as he can regarding the nature of the alleged offence, the character and background of the accused, the likelihood of his appearance for trial and such other relevant factors as will assist him in exercising his discretion. But the important

November 20, 1968
Supply-Justice
thing to remember is that under our present system there is no absolute right to bail.

speechtext: Order, please. I am sorry to advise the hon. member that his time has expired, unless it is the wish of the committee that he be allowed to continue.
Agreed.

Thank you. There is a basic principle of law which recognizes that a person should retain his freedom until he is convicted of the offence for which he has been charged. Because this is a basic principle it certainly is as applicable to the poor as it is to the rich, and it should be. It should be just as applicable to the man who does not have a cent as it was to Hal Banks, who was able to put up $25,000 in the form of bail. As was the case in respect of Hal Banks, the ability to raise a large amount of money places an accused person in a more advantageous position than an accused person who cannot raise the money and therefore must remain in jail. I suggest this is contrary to the basic principle of British justice, and I believe something should be done by way of amendment to the code to correct that unfortunate situation.
I understand the Department of Justice has the matter in hand. When the omnibus bill is brough in I hope there will be something in it to take care of both these situations, the detention of people immediately after being arrested and the broadening of the law with regard to bail, so that people will not be required after arrest to be penalized merely because they cannot find the cash necessary for bail or perhaps because they are friendless, alone in a strange place and do not have someone to go on their recognizance. These are a few things which we would hope the Minister of Justice would take into consideration when he is drafting his omnibus bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for his remarks. I shall restrain myself until later, except in respect of one point, in order to set the record completely clear with regard to the Hal Banks situation.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I must say to the hon. member that I respectfully differ with his interpretation of the law. When I learned of the reports of the statement by the United States senator from New Mexico I immediately contacted the legal officers of the crown and asked them what recourse the government had to reclaim
(Mr. McQuaid.]
Mr. Hal Banks within our jurisdiction. The law officers of the crown consulted United States counsel in New York City, in fact, the same counsel who had advised the attorney general of Ontario in the earlier extradition proceedings.
It is the view of the United States counsel, supported by the view of the law officers of the crown, that the extradition proceedings are at an end, and that the incoming United States administration cannot reverse the decision taken by Mr. Rusk and order Mr. Banks re-arrested and retained for extradition to Canada. The hon. member for Cardigan suggested that the action of the secretary of state, Dean Rusk, in refusing to sign the extradition order after Commissioner Abruzzo had committed Banks for extradition, was an executive act, not a judicial act, and therefore the judicial process had not been interrupted.
It is the view of the law officers of the crown, supported by United States counsel, that the executive act of the secretary of state, Dean Rusk, was part of the judicial process as contained in the extradition act and the extradition treaty itself. In this respect there is really no difference between the law of the United States and our own. Under our own Extradition Act, before a person who has been committed by a judge or by an extradition commissioner for surrender can be extradited, the minister, in our case the Attorney General of Canada, must so order in writing. The situation is the same in the United States. After committal for extradition or surrender, the person so committed can be extradited from the United States, but the secretary of state must so order in writing.
If in a particular case the Attorney General of Canada, or the secretary of state, being the equivalent officer under the act in the United States, should refuse to make an order for extradition we do not believe it possible-by "we" I mean the law officers of the crown, supported by the advice of United States counsel-that it can be seriously argued that the secretary of state or his successor, can later change his mind and order the person re-arrested for extradition to a foreign country.
In other words, once the discretion of the secretary of state or the Attorney General of Canada has been exercised either in favour of signing the extradition order or against it, then the proceedings have been exhausted and cannot be re-opened. I think to argue the
November 20, 19G8

contrary would mean that any person so concerned would continue in peril indefinitely, depending on changes in the administration or in policy.
I have to re-affirm, with the greatest respect to my colleague in the law, that an executive act or administrative discretion once exercised by the secretary of state of the United States, under the extradition act or the extradition treaty, cannot later be reexercised either by that same secretary of state or by a successor. Mr. Banks once having been brought into jeopardy under proper judicial process cannot be brought into jeopardy again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I read the press stories in this regard and it seems to me that the senator based his opinion on the results of some inquiries or legal opinions he obtained. This is a very serious point. I am not suggesting that the minister or his legal advisors are wrong. I have great respect for both, although I have occasionally had reason to differ with their judgment. On occasion judges have found that I was right and they were wrong.
It is well known that an information and complaint may be laid against a person who is suspected of having committed a criminal offence. A preliminary inquiry is then held; but before the time comes for a charge to be preferred in another court we often find that a stay of proceedings is entered. That stay of proceedings is an executive act. The attorney general of a province in exercising his discretion refuses to proceed with the charge in the Supreme Court or the county court, as the case may be. The entering of that stay of prosecution, the nolle prosequi, does not prevent a charge from being proceeded with against the person at a later date.
That is on all fours with this situation. I put that as a comparable case to the minister and suggest it would be of some interest to members of this committee if the minister made inquiries as to the basis of the senator's statement. It may well be that senators in the United States have access to higher priced legal talent than the department of the attorney general over there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not
know whether the United States senator for New Mexico sought legal advice, but I suggest to the hon. member for Peace River that while the attorney general might have discretion as to whether to prosecute or not if his law officers advised him there was a case, it

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He would never lay a charge in that event.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to preface my remarks by congratulating the minister on his appointment. I was rather disappointed, however, by his opening statement in respect of this important department. In speaking briefly on the Banks case, which has just been discussed, the minister stated that Mr. Banks would be placed in double jeopardy if there were to be a rehearing of this case. Double jeopardy is an old principle in respect of accused persons, but it seems to me that if Mr. Banks were retried and sent back to Canada, not only would he be in double jeopardy but the Liberal government would be in double jeopardy, because some of the members of this government sponsored Mr. Banks when he came to Canada in the first place, and some of them received contributions from the S.I.U. for their political campaigns. Therefore, there really would be double jeopardy if Mr. Banks did come back to Canada. If he does come back to Canada I hope the hon. member for York South will in future get some of those S.I.U. contributions.
I said I was disappointed in the minister's opening statement. I thought we had a minister who had a flair for reform, and one who would stand up and set forth some of the great changes he has talked about outside the house, some of which have been reported in Maclean's magazine. The minister made a rather complete presentation of the work of his department, and then made an apology for employing 72 more individuals. He has actually reached the position now that he is only a part time minister. This was the result of the reorganization measure of November, 1966. Prior to that the office of the Minister of Justice was very important. After the reorganization, the department was castrated of any real jurisdiction. Its main jurisdiction now is in respect of constitutional matters.
The Prime Minister has taken unto himself the problems associated with the constitution. He set up a task force and decided not to refer constitutional matters to any standing committee. He has kept unto himself and his officials some very important aspects of constitutional law. One might have thought that the imaginative and bright Minister of Justice would persuade the present Prime Minister to refer this matter of the constitution to a

November 20, 1968
Supply-Justice
standing committee in order that we could call experts and hear what they have to say about the delegation and redistribution of powers.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Apparently he has not been able to persuade the Prime Minister in this very important area. This is why I say he is really operating on a part time basis. He still has control of the Criminal Code. Although some parts of the Criminal Code appear to be divided with regard to jurisdiction, I am very saddened that the Minister of Justice has not taken any initiative with regard to setting up a fund from which to compensate innocent victims of criminal violence. This matter was raised by the former member for York-Humber and the principle was accepted by the government. It was referred to the standing committee on justice and legal affairs, and after a very thorough investigation I thought we had adopted the principle with regard to compensation.
There has been wide experience in this field and some of the provinces have initiated action. The lame excuse of the government is that law enforcement falls within provincial jurisdiction, and therefore the minister sidesteps the question and fails to appreciate that the federal government has contracts with eight of the ten provinces in Canada with regard to providing police services. Those services are provided on a controversial basis. The two provinces not covered are Ontario and Quebec; all other provinces are covered by contract with regard to police services. There would be nothing wrong in including in the contract sufficient money to pay compensation to innocent victims of criminal violence.
We have heard a great deal about persons who have suffered as the result of criminal violence and have received no compensation. In this respect the unimaginative minister takes no action whatsoever. He does not rise and say that the government is going to take positive action in this field, and I am greatly disappointed because of this.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?

When I have finished I will be glad to receive questions. Another area in which we are greatly disappointed is that of the expungement of criminal records. In the last session the solicitor general, in response to a question of mine during the discussion of

the estimates of the previous year, said he had laid before the cabinet a memorandum with regard to the expungement of criminal records, and the bail system. This gave encouragement to the members who had served on the standing committee on justice and legal affairs, because in respect of a bill sponsored by a Liberal member from Welland the committee studied this matter in depth, expert witnesses were called and a report was made to the house with regard to the expungement of criminal records. The same thing applied to bail. Here we had the undertaking of the former solicitor general that the matter was in memorandum form before the cabinet for decision. We had encouragement in this respect.
What happened? An election was called. We now have a new cabinet and no initiative has been taken by the Minister of Justice or the Solicitor General with regard to action in these very important fields. This is something with regard to which the part time Minister of Justice could take a real stride forward in introducing legislation in the house.
I am now going to give the minister more suggestions with regard to things he could do, and thereby make himself a name in Canadian history, as one who never stood in the background but was always in the forefront of reform. There is the question of the Expropriation Act. You will notice, Mr. Chairman, that in this session the hon. member for Peel South introduced a motion with regard to the setting up of a new Expropriation Act. The motion was adopted, and accepted by the government in principle.
The minister has said-this is in the throne speech, and statements made by the minister-that he intends to bring forth legislation with regard to a new Expropriation Act. Perhaps you do not know this, Mr. Chairman, but it is very significant that back in 1962 this government also brought forth an act respecting the expropriation of land. This matter was started in 1962, but here we are in 1968 and no measure has been placed before the house. Surely the Minister of Justice, a very bright, intelligent and active minister, could bring forth this measure in a matter of days and have it referred to the standing committee on justice and legal affairs.
The hon. member for Peel South is very interested in this act, because if the airport in Toronto is extended there will be a great deal of land expropriation. If this measure is not introduced by the time the expropriation
November 20, 1968

takes place, the hon. member is in real jeopardy with regard to being re-elected next time, because he knows how old the other act is. Since 1889 there have not been any amendments to the Expropriation Act. The hon. member knows that the important item with regard to compensation is giving notice to landowners in respect of expropriation. These are the two main areas in the Expropriation Act, and they were pretty fully covered in the 1962 act. There is no reason why the Minister of Justice cannot at this time bring forth a new act and have it referred to the standing committee.
The next question I wish to discuss is that of marijuana, Mr. Chairman. If ever an issue has been debated recently it is the issue of marijuana. We find there is divided jurisdiction between the Minister of National Health and Welfare and possibly the Solicitor General, or it may be the Minister of Justice, if he is in charge of the drug and narcotics control act. We have had evidence from the deputy commissioner of the R.C.M.P. of an alarming increase in marijuana convictions. It should be fully appreciated that 80 per cent of this increase applies to young men and young women between the ages of 16 and 25. This was the statement of the deputy commissioner.
One has to appreciate what a conviction means to a young person. It means he has difficulty with regard to obtaining employment, with regard to travel and bonding. Yet here we sit, with the Minister of Justice taking no action with regard to a proper amendment to the act. No action is taken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and we have a statement by the Solicitor General that no action will be taken during this session. This is a field into which the Minister of Justice should step, and correct the situation, because it has a serious effect on our young people.
The next item with which I wish to deal is that of corporal punishment. Every time I pick up the Criminal Code and read section 641 I realize that this section must have been drafted back in medieval times, in the 16th century. I will read section 641 which falls under the heading of "whipping":
Where a person is liable to be sentenced to be whipped, the court may sentence him to be whipped on one, two or three occasions within the limits of the prison in which he is confined.
Is it not time that our Minister of Justice took some steps with regard to corporal punishment? The John Howard Society says
Supply-Justice
that the approach to criminal law today should be that of rehabilitation and reform rather than that of revenge. This is the approach that is dear to the hearts not only of the members of the John Howard Society but also the hearts of social workers throughout the country. Reform in this matter of corporal punishment is an area in which we would have no difficulty in getting the full support of the house. The days have long passed when we resorted to these cruel and barbaric methods.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The other item which I am sure falls under the minister's jurisdiction is that of the uniformity of sentencing. There has been a wide disparity in sentencing throughout the country, and if there were some guide lines within the Criminal Code to ensure some measure of uniformity, justice would be applied equally throughout the country. I will ask the Minister of Justice to take immediate action with regard to sentencing, which I am sure falls within his area of jurisdiction, and to bring this legislation up to date. It needs it.
Another matter which I should like to mention is the review of the Criminal Code. I thought the minister would say that since this is an electronic age it is necessary to have legislation with regard to electronic devices for bugging, that he would make a statement on it and refer it to a standing committee, or else give us a promise of legislation. However, not a word was mentioned.
The other matter which I should like to mention regards the insanity rules in the Criminal Code. It has been a long time since any change has been made in the M'Naghten rules on insanity and surely, in view of the progress in the field of psychology and psychiatry, it is time we made some changes in those rules.
Another matter regards the appeal procedure in summary convictions. Many people have found those provisions very difficult to comply with and often cases are thrown out on very technical grounds. It is important that the poor and the innocent are not convicted unfairly.
Another matter is that of vagrancy. This has been a charge under the Criminal Code used by the police as a holding charge, with regard to some other offence which the police may want to apply. I believe the minister should take a forward look at this matter of vagrancy and change this section so as to stop the police from using it as a holding charge.

It is high time that this was done, because the last revision of the statutes of Canada was made back in 1952, and from 1952 to the present time we have had annual statutes. students are concerned-just to mention one instance and to repeat the expression used a minute ago by the minister-it was inconvenient. For example, I would like this committee-which, as suggested by the minister, would be established in the near future-to study the structure of judicial or quasi-judicial organizations. At the present time, we do not know the nature of that structure, it is rather topsy-turvy, to use a common expression, since one cannot make head or tail of it. I see that the minister is smiling and I know that he agrees with me.
I think that is is essential to review the organization of those administrative tribunals, in order to get acquainted with those judicial and quasi-judicial organizations, and to consider as well the status of the members and support personnel of those organizations.

Moreover, certain members do not know what they are doing in this respect; they do not understand the role they are to play. They admit themselves that their personal jurisdiction sometimes overlaps with that of their neighbours or colleagues. There is total confusion. Therefore, that is the first point which should be studied by the committee.
Secondly, and I think the hon. minister will again agree with me, this special committee on administrative courts should examine their territorial jurisdiction and the sanctions of rules of competence. That does not need much explanation.
Third, I should like this committee to study the procedure to be followed in appearing before these administrative courts, so that the rights of every citizen, every person under the jurisdiction of the courts, may be properly protected and a more uniform procedure established. I think that is a fundamental point, Mr. Chairman. The rights of every individual under the jurisdiction of the court must be clearly protected, so that justice may not be a question of money, prestige, resources, the reputation of a businessman or whatever, but really a human question. Everyone should be on the same footing before the law, which is supreme.
I would also like the committee to study thoroughly the advisability of establishing a court of appeal from the decisions of lower courts dealing with administrative matters. The representations I am now making to the minister are valid, and the minister will be able to consider them in due time, since they could be a part of the study made by the special committee.
Finally, I would like this committee on administrative courts to examine thoroughly the advisability of appointing an ombudsman or using some other method to ensure that the rights of every individual under the jurisdiction of the courts are fully protected against encroaching administration.
Mr. Chairman, I think we have set up a program of work for the special committee which could be appointed to study the structure of the administrative courts. These five specific points present a whole program of activities, and hon. members would be very glad with the opportunity of studying the matters in depth, in order to ensure an equitable treatment for every individual coming under the jurisdiction of the courts and to see to it that the justice dispensed is not unjust.
Mr. Chairman, I have the English translation of the remarks I have just addressed to 
the minister about those administrative courts.
I have even put that matter in a notice of motion which he will find in the order paper.
I will therefore give him immediately an English copy of what I have just said about setting up a special committee, so that if he is getting ready to reply immediately or to make a few definite comments on those points, he might do so in the language in which he is most fluent.
I should like to be able some day, Mr. Chairman, to deliver a speech in English. A while ago, I had decided to do so in the case of my very short speech, but I would rather attend for some time the government language school before making my first attemps in that language, as I cannot "skate" as easily in English as in French.
One must realize that this word may have different meanings. To "skate" like the member for Temiscamingue and to "skate" like the member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) are two very different things, Mr. Chairman.
I should like to say to the minister that I appreciate his work in the Department of Justice and I am not necessarily of the opinion of the member who spoke before me and who said that the minister is a mini-minister or a part-time minister.
I think he is doing an excellent job, but he should deal with some fundamental matters. One would be, of course, the setting up of a special committee on administrative courts. I am most anxious to hear his comments.

Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the minister upon the energetic and capable leadership he has given this house and country in the field of criminal reform.
The hon. member for Broadview spoke about compensation for victims of crime. If the minister were to heed the hon. member's exhortations, however, I feel a great burden would be put on him to legislate with respect to something that falls clearly within provincial jurisdiction. The minister would be wasting his already scarce time on something over which he has no jurisdiction.
Today I wish to make two points. The first is a suggestion that the summary conviction appeal procedure be streamlined or made simpler and easier for those who fall prey to the technical barriers which confound the path of one who appeals. I suggest that subsection 3 of section 722 of the Criminal Code,
November 20, 1968

which deals with appeals from summary conviction courts to county judges, be amended to read:
The appeal court may at any time up to the date of the hearing of the appeal, waive any defects or omissions in the appeal process when the court considers it in the best interests of justice so to do.
I think that such a provision would remove some of the technical barriers people encounter through failure to have an affidavit sworn, to find a magistrate, who may be away on his summer holidays, or to raise sufficient costs. This would also cover many other matters urgently requiring attention.
I have had 18 years experience in practise of the criminal law, both in defence and, latterly, as a crown prosecutor. I have had a chance to view the matter and I have seen many difficulties of the nature I have described. I shall refer to only one case, that of Regina v. Amyot, 1968 Ontario reports, volume 2, at page 626. There an Ontario county judge found he had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal because the listing of the appeal was not properly posted at a certain place in the court house. If the appeal had been listed inside the court office it could have been heard; but since some clerk placed the list outside the court room, the appeal could not be heard. That does not strike me as being the course of true justice and I am sure the minister will be interested in assisting in this field of reform.
My second point deals with prelimary hearings. I urge the minister to consider the saving of money and the convenience of witnesses which might result from our adopting the British use of depositions. For instance, if a witness is to be called merely to give a formal statement such as, "Yes, I picked up a document at 5 a.m. on November 12," that statement could be reduced to a simple deposition or affidavit, and filed. Of course defence counsel would still have the privilege of calling that witness. I submit that in many thousand of cases in this country much money could be saved and many people con-venienced by adopting such a system.

Mr. Chairman, I have only one comment to make, or only one question to direct to the Minister of Justice. He must realize, as we all realize, that there is a controversy about the widespread use of marijuana. Marijuana itself does not seem to be a particularly dangerous drug. The greatest danger lies in the fact that a user may 29180-189
Supply-Justice
move on to more dangerous substances. There is however remarkably little medical literature about its effects.
In February, 1968, and again in March, 1968, the then Minister of Justice when replying to questions said that the policy of the government was to adopt what might be called the hard line. Since then there has been much comment and controversy. Suggestions have been made that this approach is hard and harsh. Speaking in Regina to the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association, the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that narcotics legislation might be amended or modified by introducing a marijuana control bill.
The question of narcotics has long exercised our officials. I think it is well known that the intent of the Narcotic Control Act is to control the widespread use of drugs. I think it is conceded that we ought to be more concerned with distributors of these harmful substances than with users. In other words, there ought to be changes in the act which would remove the profit that pushers may make by selling drugs. Perhaps the law ought to provide more severe penalties for those who push drugs. There has also been a suggestion that under the new legislation it may not be necessary to lay a formal charge of possession against those who possess drugs. In any event, if the narcotics legislation were changed I suggest it might be a good idea not to punish the users of marijuana as severely as the pushers who traffic in the drug for profit.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MODIFY COMPOSITION OF COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to amending the provisions of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act so as to modify the composition of the various commissions with a view to obtaining more logical and equitable redistribution of constituency boundaries and to provide that any and all reports and recommendations of the said commissions shall be accompanied by full and detailed reasons for any proposed changes, all of which changes and the reasons therefore shall be debatable in this house.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on proposals that have been submitted during recent years, particularly in the course of the first revision by a commission established for reviewing the electoral boundaries, as required by law. I believe that every one of us, in the light of his own experience, will be able to determine the results that have been achieved.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

The purpose of my motion is to persuade the government to introduce amendments to the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, in particular to sections 6, 13, 18 and 20-and there may be some other sections related to these. You were good enough, Mr. Speaker, to read out the terms of the resolution so I shall not repeat it. The main purpose is to consider the composition of these commissions, their method of performance, the principles upon which they proceeded, the nature of their reports and the manner in which these reports were handled in the house.
I bring up this subject with some diffidence. I wish it to be clearly understood by hon. members that I make no reflection whatsoever on the ridings which they represent. Those who have been elected to this house for the first time will, naturally, have no experience of the long and difficult debates on this subject which took place in 1964 and 1965. Most of them will not have gone over the public hearings, the subsequent debate on the reports, and the representations made when those reports were adopted by the house.
Regardless of the experience which may have been reflected in various places, I would
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]

say that the last redistribution, the first under the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, left much to be desired. In some provinces it could be termed a disaster. I believe every canon of good sense was traversed. One of my former collagues said he thought that in many areas there had been gerrymandering by lack of knowledge and perhaps by some incompetence. I would agree with him. People in the Province of Alberta, in particular, are singularly bitter about the results; we thought they were among the poorest. I am telling the commissioners nothing new when I say this; I have told them so before. In other places they were adequate, but no more.
There was supposedly a professed independence among the commissioners. But as a result of some of the decisions in these connections no other conclusion can be drawn but that some of the divisions had been motivated by political considerations of the type they were not supposed to have. Frankly, there was some gerrymandering in certain districts and some hiving off, and no one will explain them to me in any other way because I could go into those particular districts and show that there is no rhyme or reason about the decisions-no reason of demography, no reason of social contact, that the people go to the same market town, that the children come from the same school district, that they are on the same side of a major river, or anything of that sort. There was a hiving off.
I suggest that in the main the act unfortunately lays too great emphasis on the so-called equality of numbers, with a tolerance of 25 per cent up and down. Those of us who were here will recall there was a great deal of debate about the extent of that tolerance before we finally settled on 25 per cent. Members of two commissions have told me: Thank goodness parliament showed a minimum of good sense in going so far. In their provinces it would have been impossible to operate on any legal tolerance less than that figure. After all, 25 per cent was not mandatory; the commissions could work within a tolerance of 5 per cent up and down if peculiar circumstances dictated it.
Section 13 did provide for looking to demography, to special geographical features, to elements of growth in suburban communities, difficult boundaries and so on. In the main, these were ignored. Take my own riding, so that I do not point a finger at anyone else. I was left with a strip of land two miles deep and ten miles long which straddled the northern edge of the whole city of Edmonton.
November 20, 1968

I do not object to the people there. I had this territory before, though much more. But this two miles is now an area of development on the north of Edmonton from Edmonton centre. My neighbours between the centre of the city and Edmonton east, to the east of the centre, are inhibited in growth; they have no new area of development.
The northern strip is being developed at a great rate at the present time, particularly next to Edmonton east. My colleague from Edmonton East (Mr. Skoreyko) lives there; he bought and built there because he knew this area was supposed to be included in his constituency. But it was not. The net result is that people who are on the far northeast part of the city are attached to the people living in the far western part of the city though there is no contact whatsoever beyond the fact that they live in the city of Edmonton.
I can tell you the reason why. There was in between a military base and they wanted to leave it in my constituency; they felt that 300 or 400 Liberal votes coming from that base would perhaps work to somebody else's advantage. There is no other reason for leaving that two mile strip.

speechtext:
However, it did not work out that way. Never did that traverse the minds of the commissioners? Well, knowing the commissioners as I do, I shall leave it at that.
The complicated constituency boundaries resulted in confusion for civilian voters. May I say, also, that I was able to examine the lists of all servicemen west of the Great Lakes, and I know from the scrutineers connected with the service vote that hundreds and hundreds of ballots were spoiled because of the complicated boundaries which resulted from the commissioners' decisions in many instances. I am thinking particularly of the Province of Alberta-leave it to others who wish to talk about their own experience.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Ridings made no sense geographically, leading to very difficult election campaigns. Often, no interior roads existed. We have one constituency that stretches along the eastern slope of the mountains, running some 450 miles, I would say, from the United States boundary, and 36 miles south of the city of Grand Prairie. There is not a road running directly through that constituency. The people in it have no community of interest. My
2995
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act colleague from Athabasca has to get around his constituency in an aircraft because there are no direct roads, unless he goes through four or five other constituencies.
It seems to me that a constituency should be so designed that its member shall be able to have reasonably quick access to his constituents and they to him. There should be a form of unit. Instead of that we get these conglomerations designed strictly on the basis of so-called population squares that head off to nowhere. I told the chairman of our commission in Alberta that as punishment the commission should have to travel the boundaries of all the constituencies it designed.
I believe that section 13 has to be amended in order to get the emphasis removed from being placed purely on numbers, and to give effect to demographic reasons. During the past election, and I think this is a question of political science, we were asking for the involvement of the people with government. Yet the last redistribution of constituencies has made it practically impossible for many constituents to have contact with their members, or members with their constituents, or even contact among the constituents themselves.
Then there is the question of the commission reports. I always feel that he who desires to make a change has the onus of proof upon him and must advance the reasons for the change. We did not see anything like that in the last redistribution. We were simply given a report and a map with legal descriptions, on the basis that they had been handed down from on high. I found the attitude of some of the commissioners to be as though they had been commissioned by God and were handing down an edict. Their attitude was that anyone who dared to criticize their decision just did not know what he was talking about, and any appearance made at a commission's public hearings was a nuisance to the commission.
I found that the commissions had gone to work on the basis of paper furnished to them by the staff of the boundaries commissioner who had been working on a sort of jigsaw puzzle fitting the pieces together. I believe that hon. members and the public generally are interested in putting viable political units together. In a growing city riding no one can say, "We can put this section in there because we think we have more Liberal",-or Tory, or Social Credit or N.D.P.-"votes in it." This is nonsense. There is no pattern of voting in newly developing areas. It cannot be forecast.
2996	COMMONS
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act
Certainly there has to be some equality of numbers or relationship of numbers, but I am sure hon. members will agree it is a better principle to establish a political unit upon reasons of demography, geography, community of interest and other factors.
As provided in the act, a commission's reports and reasons should come before the house if there is objection to the redistribution in the required volume. The reports and reasons then become available for examination. As a result of the last redistribution my colleague from Calgary North and other hon. members, including myself, sought to obtain the records and memoranda on which redistribution commissions operate, in order to see what on earth led to this blessed mess; but this was denied on a fine legal point. Then the motion was transferred for debate and got lost in the complexities of the legislative machinery.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members will want to examine this question. I have proposed this motion at this time for serious consideration. I have not spoken about the composition of the commissions, although I think my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre may wish to talk about that. I think difficulty in this connection could be avoided if as originally proposed and provided in the act, and as we thought we were getting, a representative would be recommended by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and one by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to sit on a commission. This would eliminate any, shall we say, political jiggery-pokery.

speechtext: That is a good word.

speechtext:
Or shenanigans-whatever word you want to use. I am sure that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) can come up with somewhat more colourful ones but he knows fully what I mean. If that were done there would be a stand-off respecting the question of political influence. There would certainly be a greater understanding of political principles and of a political unit than was demonstrated by most of the commissions during the last redistribution.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say we want to have something better in the composition of commissions. We want to have something better in the way of the principles upon which a redistribution shall take place, and we want to have the reports of commissions so that we can see just why certain constituencies were put together, thus placing the onus for

DEBATES	November 20, 1968
changes upon the commissions. They have to justify the changes. They may want to make a change by saying, "In this district the population has changed." That is perfectly valid. This is a reason; but there are other reasons that must be included.
To talk to one of these commissions and try to justify your own opinions is almost like beating a pillow, and a very soft pillow at that. I do not think I have seen anything work so arbitrarily and poorly as the last electoral redistributions. Therefore I urge hon. members to consider my motion, and I trust in its ultimate adoption.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion which is now before us seeks to amend the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and therefore, hopefully, to establish at some future time more logical and equitable redistribution of constituency boundaries. To this end it asks that all changes and the reasons therefor be debatable in this house before being put into effect. Certainly every member of this chamber believes that constituency boundaries should make some kind of reasonable sense, and that no constituency should be more burdensome or difficult to represent than any other. What
November 20, 1968
we would like and what is possible, however, never converge, but like parallel lines run merrily together into infinity. Logical and equitable constituencies are hardly possible in a nation like ours, which in itself is neither particularly logical nor equitable. It has been said that some countries have too much history but that Canada has too much geography. Well, that may be so, but despite seemingly insurmountable geographical obstacles our ancestors who came from here, there and everywhere forged an unlikely nation in the northern part of this continent. Canada may not accurately be called a logical political, geographic or historical entity, yet it survives and even thrives.
If our nation cannot be described as a logical outcome of historical forces, neither can it be described today as a shining example of equality. We continue to be troubled by glaring inequalities of economic well-being and opportunity which exist from region to region, and within our major cities as well. Thus, it may be said that we have the kind and size of constituencies which we deserve, living in a nation such as ours, constituencies which are as illogical and inequitable as this nation itself. Certainly, when it comes to the question of size, as the member for Thunder Bay I have something to complain about. This riding is much too vast for any one man to represent adequately, even if he were a reasonable facsimile of Paul Bunyan, which I am not. A region which includes 155,000 square miles is a huge area to cover adequately, even during the term of a single parliament. Yet in all this expansive acreage there are only 55,000 people, of whom approximately
26,000	are eligible to vote. If I subscribe to the democratic principle of one man one vote, which I do as nearly as it is possible to hold to that principle, it is neither reasonable nor logical for me to expect my constituency to shrink in size unless-and this is something for which we in northern Ontario press all the time-through a vigorous program of regional development we can attract thousands of people into northwestern Ontario to enjoy with us the good life there, and help us develop our almost limitless natural resources.
The mere alteration of constituency boundaries really is no certain guarantee of greater equity for either members or the constituents whom they represent. To this end it does seem reasonable to make a small suggestion to the commissioners of internal economy. I am sure my hon. friends from Kenora-Rainy
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act River, Algoma East, Cochrane, and many others, would agree with me when I suggest that those who represent extremely large rural ridings should be given some extra financial consideration to assist them in meeting the extremely heavy expenses which are incurred in representing such constituencies. The people of my riding are a great distance from most departments of government. Therefore they rely very heavily upon their member, whom they expect to see regularly and often. I am prepared to agree that in the constituency of Thunder Bay there are certain illogical aspects which we would like to see changed. For example the southwest corner of the riding includes people who live near the outskirts of Fort Frances, a town which lies within the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River. Naturally these people look to Fort Frances as their centre for commerce and recreation. It follows therefore that logically they should reside in the same federal constituency as the townsfolk. Again, my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River has included in his riding the town of Sioux Lookout, which is linked in its educational system under the new reorganization of school districts in Ontario with the town of Dryden, the largest community in Thunder Bay.
In order to reach Sioux Lookout the member from Kenora-Rainy River must follow a fairly long route through Thunder Bay. Since we wear the same political colours there is no problem, but there is great inconvenience for the member, and the charge of illogical redistribution is probably justified. Further, a constituency like Thunder Bay is faced with the problems of communication which fight against the existence of a community of interest or common concern, and it is not logical that people in one constituency should be so isolated from each other that they are unaware of what people in other parts of the constituency are doing, or of what problems there may be in another part of the constituency. There is no single radio or television outlet which serves the whole area. No one newspaper is read by the majority of the constituents. Some look to Winnipeg, others to the lakehead, and still others to Toronto as their chief urban centre.
As I have indicated, we in northwestern Ontario certainly are not at a loss to offer full and detailed reasons for a more logical and equitable redistribution of some of our constituency boundaries. There is, however, one very troublesome aspect to this notice of motion which prevents me lending support to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
2998	COMMONS
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act Lambert). The troublesome clause contains the suggestion that in the future full and detailed reasons for any proposed increase shall be debatable in this house. I can imagine a very long debate in which each member would want to have the opportunity to explain why the particular reasons given for the changes in his constituency are neither right nor justified.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
It seems to me, however, that this house has more pressing, urgent and serious matters to consider. There is not enough time at our disposal for us to become bogged down in trivialities, to major in minors. We should in fact count ourselves fortunate that we are spared the laborious effort of having to consider the justification for the boundary lines of 264 constituencies. What member is there who would not argue long and strong that some particular city block, some village or town or some small region does not properly or logically fit into his constituency? The motivations for such reasoning would be many and varied, but among them would be a feeling of hostility for that city block, village, town or small area which happened to be mainly of a political persuasion different from that of the member. How pleasant it would be to attempt to jettison those troublesome voters who live in darkness and have not yet seen the light of our political wisdom.
No, Mr. Speaker this house has no time for such pettiness. The Canadian people expect us to get on with the job of governing. Even now, the proceedings of this house are all too tedious and tardy. Time is propelling us rapidly and irresistibly into the 21st century, yet our nation is still burdened with worn-out laws, and in so many ways we are still basically an underdeveloped nation.
I conclude by saying, let us leave the problems of constituency boundaries to non-political commissions; let us put up with the few illogical or inequitable aspects which trouble us; let us not waste the precious time of this assembly, but rather, let us push on with the job of building Canada into a just and modern nation which is governed in a way that is relevant to the needs of the present and the future.
