Mr. Speaker, I recognize that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has a grievance. In fact, I well recall the expressed feelings of most of the Alberta members of the last parliament about the redistribution map in respect of that province. I think I would only be facing reality if I admitted there was a general feeling on the part of those members that they all had grievances.
The hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner) has just reflected the fact that there are other members in the house who likewise have grievances in respect of certain aspects of the boundaries of their constituencies. I must say, however, that I do not agree with the solution to the problem proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West. We sit near each other and we have to be good friends whether we want to be or not, but I do not like the retrogressive step proposed in this resolution.
It is my feeling that one of the most progressive steps of a political nature parliament ever took was the step we took when we ended 100 years of political, partisan gerrymandering that went on every time we had distribution.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MODIFY COMPOSITION OF COMMISSIONS
speechtext: They only do it a different way now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MODIFY COMPOSITION OF COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
was a member of two or three parliamentary committees that engaged in redistribution, so I know something of what that experience is, and I certainly do not want to go through it again. It is a proper procedure that the boundaries of our constituencies should be determined by some body other than the members who run for and seek to represent those ridings, and I hope it will stay that way.
There are one or two things the hon. member for Edmonton West said with which I may have some sympathy, but I must dissociate myself from some of his remarks. He has indicated that he said to the commissioners in

November 20, 1968	COMMONS
the province of Alberta what he thought of their work. I have to leave to him and the Alberta members what their experience may have been with their commissioners. Perhaps I am one of the fortunate ones. I come from a province where we had redistribution by an independent commission on a provincial basis before this was brought in federally. Not only did we have this take place provincially ahead of the federal scheme, but the same people who were assigned to do the provincial job were called upon to do the federal job. The only change was to add the representation commissioner, Mr. Castonguay. So we had experienced people do the job in Manitoba.
I do not suggest there are not some complaints that members from Manitoba could make, and I do not think any map could be drawn that would be perfect to anyone. But I am prepared to say that the Manitoba division as a result of the last redistribution seems to be about as good as it could be, and as fair as possible to all concerned. I have heard rumblings of discontent in one or two other parts of Canada, but surely that is a small price to pay for getting it established that the boundaries of our constituencies are determined by someone other than the members who are affected, who after all have a conflict of interest.
The hon. member for Edmonton West talked about the way in which these commissioners brought in their reports, as though they were edicts from on high. I suppose that could be said about any commission or body which has been given a delegated authority. Whenever they make their reports they seem to be edicts. But let me point out that these commissions have only the authority given to them by a parliamentary statute. Let me also point out that in the statute we provided that the commissioners had to publish their first or preliminary reports and then hold hearings at which the public might appear and make representations. Mr. Speaker, at first glance, it would seem that the motion of the member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is well founded. However, considering the argument of the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I feel some reservations should be made.
I should therefore like to express, at least, the reactions of the people in my riding with regard to the new electoral map. In my riding of Champlain, there is some astonishment. Indeed, some people did not even realize, before June 25, that they were voting in the Champlain riding only. Obviously-it was to be expected-people cannot adapt to a new situation within a few months.
However, I believe most sincerely that the limits of the Champlain riding were not set up in a scientific and logical way. In fact, I wonder why the recommendations made by the municipalities and the people concerned were not taken into consideration, as in the case of the municipality of Portneuf which made representations to the commission-I think that this cost approximately $2,000 to $3,000-and evidently it did not win its case, so that today, it is annoying for the town of Portneuf to be in the constituency of Champlain. I think it will take many years before people get used to writing "Portneuf, county of Champlain".
Surely this is a striking case. We can see that there is a lack of logic in that, since the twenty municipalities of the county of Portneuf, unsatisfied with the new boundaries, went over to the county of Champlain. I wonder if the people living in those constituencies should not have something to say about it. They thought that some politicking was involved and they decided to have their revenge saying: "Instead of one Creditiste member, we will have two." This is why they voted for the Credistites in the constituency of Portneuf as well as in that of Champlain.
I wanted to make those few comments to point out that those commissions should take a little more into account the views of the people. The constituency of Champlain extending from Portneuf to Cap-de-la-Madeleine to the south and north as far as

But that does not mean that decisions should be taken without consulting with the voters and the people concerned in order to know if they are interested and if they have any reasons to be listed in such a riding rather than another.
Mr. Speaker, I think that in my riding, they have used arbitrary limits such as a river. The commission has failed to find out if the people really wanted to be in such a riding instead of another and if, by normal attraction, for geographical reasons or through habit, they were going to my riding, for example, to Jonquiere, rather than Chicoutimi or Alma.
Mr. Speaker, surely there are no easy or perfect solutions. In my opinion, if the commission had obtained further information from the constituents, I think a more equitable decision would have been reached.
